question: How do soy and palm come to dominate the world's fats — and why does the argument over which fat is healthy never end?
thesis: Since 1960 fat has been fought over on two fronts. In the West the argument is about health: official advice turns against fat, then against trans fats, and the substitutes move the world’s supply toward soy and palm. In the tropics palm oil, driven by Malaysia’s planned growth and India’s appetite, becomes the cheapest fat on earth, with fires, supply chains and plantation communities as its cost; whaling ends, and olive oil becomes a field of fraud.

big_ideas.title: Health advice turns against fat, then against trans fats
big_ideas.text: The McGovern committee’s Dietary Goals urge Americans to eat less fat in 1977, the Women’s Health Initiative later finds no benefit from a low-fat diet, trans fats are named as a danger from 1990, and Denmark and the FDA act in 2003. Olestra, a fat the body cannot absorb, is the industry’s own answer.

big_ideas.title: Soy and palm become the two giants
big_ideas.text: Soybean oil becomes the world’s most used oil and America’s hydrogenated one, while Malaysia’s palm oil grows twenty-five-fold in twenty years and India becomes its biggest buyer. The trans-fat ban hands palm oil an American market, and canola and high-oleic sunflower join them.

big_ideas.title: Palm oil’s costs are fires, supply chains and plantation communities
big_ideas.text: Renewable-fuel mandates turn palm oil into diesel, a few firms trade much of the world’s supply, the fires of 2015 burn six million acres of forest, and communities around Socfin’s plantations seek reparations.

big_ideas.title: Olive oil is revived, and counterfeited
big_ideas.text: Olive oil spreads to California and Australia and the United States overtakes Greece as a consumer, while the record is full of fraud: a rapeseed oil that kills 800 in Spain, a hazelnut-oil tanker at Barletta, alleged Tunisian oil in Puglia, a New Jersey seizure, a voluntary American standard and the West Bank’s ‘Olive Wars’.

big_ideas.title: Elsewhere, fat follows other rules
big_ideas.text: Japan adds meat, dairy products and oil to a rice diet, India’s vanaspati lives under price control, the Middle East imports its shortening as palm oil, East African herders and Tibetans live on milk fat, and sesame is an export crop in Ethiopia and a paste in Turkey.

threads.title: Fat, health and the law
threads.claim: Advice swings from ‘eat less fat’ to ‘beware of trans fats’, and the state follows the science, late.

beats.text: Procter & Gamble’s olestra, a fat the body cannot absorb, is found by accident in 1968.
The McGovern committee’s Dietary Goals urge Americans to eat less fat and cholesterol.
Mensink and Katan, then Willett, name trans fats as a danger.
The Women’s Health Initiative finds no benefit from a low-fat diet.
The FDA approves olestra on the eve of its patent’s expiry.
Denmark limits trans fats and the FDA requires them on the label.
Fred Kummerow, aged 98, petitions the FDA to ban trans fats.
The FDA moves to ban partially hydrogenated oils, and the WHO plans to end them.

threads.title: The rise of palm oil
threads.claim: A state-backed smallholder scheme in Malaysia becomes the world’s main source of cheap fat.

beats.text: Malaysia replants old rubber estates with oil palm under FELDA’s smallholder schemes.
Malaysia’s palm-oil output grows more than twenty-five-fold in twenty years.
The Palmolive campaign prefigures palm oil’s American rise, imports growing from 29,000 tons.
The American Soybean Association brands palm and coconut oil ‘unhealthy tropical grease’.
Full-page newspaper advertisements portray tropical oils as a threat to health.
India goes from buying 30,000 tonnes of palm oil to 9.2 million tonnes.
The trans-fat ban gives palm oil an American market: imports rise 263 per cent.

threads.title: The cost of the palm frontier
threads.claim: Fuel mandates and global traders raise demand while forests burn and workers seek redress.

beats.text: US and EU renewable-fuel mandates turn palm oil into diesel.
Communities around Socfin plantations seek reparations in Cameroon and Sierra Leone.
Wilmar trades about 40 per cent of the world’s palm oil, with supplying mills linked to deforestation.
Fires traced to oil-palm plantations burn over six million acres in Sumatra and Borneo.

threads.title: Replacements: soy, canola, sunflower and the end of whale oil
threads.claim: Vegetable oils take over from the whale and from each other.

beats.text: The last whaling for profit ends under quotas, the moratorium and the competition of vegetable oils.
Soybean oil, once minor, becomes the world’s most used oil, mostly hydrogenated in America.
Canadian breeders produce an edible rapeseed, renamed canola, on a web lead that is not verified.
High-oleic sunflower oil originates in Russia by selective breeding and mutagenesis.
The International Whaling Commission passes a moratorium on commercial whaling.

threads.title: Olive oil: revival and fraud
threads.claim: A prestige oil grows in new countries and attracts counterfeiters and political quarrels.

beats.text: Rapeseed oil sold as olive oil causes the toxic oil syndrome in Spain, killing about 800.
California and Australia start new olive-oil industries, and America overtakes Greece as a market.
Investigators say Turkish hazelnut oil became ‘Greek olive oil’ at Barletta.
Italian investigators allege non-EU oil passed off as Italian in Puglia.
West Bank olive groves are burned, uprooted and cut off in the ‘Olive Wars’, as Mueller reports.
Federal marshals seize 87,000 litres of supposed extra virgin oil in New Jersey.
The USDA’s new olive-oil standard is voluntary and unenforced.

threads.title: Fat beyond the factory
threads.claim: Outside the Western health argument and the palm trade, diets and fat economies follow older rules.

beats.text: Japan adds meat, dairy products, fats and oils to a rice diet.
Price controls squeeze Unilever’s vanaspati margin in India to 4 per cent.
Yak butter goes into tsocha and the lamps of the lamaseries in Tibet and the Himalaya.
Egypt, Iraq, Turkey and Saudi Arabia import palm oil for their shortening.
Milk supplies three-quarters of the calories of the Rendille and is the staple fat of many herders.
Ethiopia presses sesame in camel-driven mortars and exports most of its crop.
Turkey grinds its sesame into tahin and no longer presses it.
China grows a fifth of the world’s sesame and presses two-thirds of it for oil.

turning_points.text: Malaysia’s palm-oil expansion begins in earnest.
The Dietary Goals say eat less fat.
Adulterated oil sold as olive oil kills 800 in Spain.
Soybean growers launch the war on tropical oils.
A clinical trial names trans fats a danger.
The Women’s Health Initiative begins; it finds no benefit from low fat.
Denmark limits trans fats; the FDA requires labels.
The trans-fat rules open an American market to palm oil.
The FDA proposes to ban partially hydrogenated oils.
Palm-plantation fires burn six million acres.

text: Four entries: Denmark’s trans-fat limit, Mensink and Katan’s trans-fat study, Spain’s toxic oil syndrome and Russia’s high-oleic sunflower ([[o2]], [[th1]], [[l3]], [[te2]]). Brussels appears in the worldwide biofuel entry.

Four entries: the palm-oil imports of Egypt, Iraq, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, from Kiple’s table ([[ec10]]); Turkey’s sesame, ground into tahin while the oil presses stand idle ([[ec14]]); Turkish hazelnut oil relabelled as Greek olive oil in 1991, in the investigators’ account; and the West Bank’s ‘Olive Wars’, with their disputed tree counts and the shared Muslim–Christian harvest ([[x3]], [[c2]]), both from Mueller. Egypt’s own oil economy is otherwise missing.

The palm frontier: FELDA and Tenera, Malaysia’s boom, India as the biggest buyer, the Singapore–Indonesia supply chain and the 2015 fires ([[ec7]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x1]], [[w1]]); India’s vanaspati under price control ([[ec9]]); and Japan, whose rice diet adds meat, dairy products, fats and oils from the 1960s ([[ec8]]). China and Korea as buyers of soy and oil have no entry. Yak butter, the butter tea of Tibet and the Himalaya and the butter lamps of the lamaseries are in Kiple’s yak chapter ([[ec12]]). China first in sesame, with two-thirds of the crop pressed for oil, and Thailand’s sesame oil for massage, are in the *Sesame* volume ([[ec15]]).

Three entries: a Tunisian cargo relabelled as Italian, in Mueller’s account of allegations ([[x2]]); the herders of northern Kenya and Sudan, for whom camel and cattle milk is the staple fat ([[ec11]]); and Ethiopia’s sesame, pressed in camel-driven mortars and eaten as paste in fasting stews ([[ec13]]). The palm and oilseed economies of West and Central Africa themselves are missing.

Fourteen entries, mostly federal and corporate: the Dietary Goals, the tropical oils war, Olestra, the olive-oil standard, the New Jersey seizure, soy’s rise, the trans-fat ban and palm’s American market, the Women’s Health Initiative, Palmolive’s advertising, Kummerow’s petition, canola, and the new olive oil of California — and one that is not: the Nuxalk Nation’s own fermenting-and-cooking-box tradition for eulachon grease on the Bella Coola River, the only Indigenous fat economy this folio documents directly ([[o1]], [[c1]], [[o4]], [[o5]], [[o8]], [[ec1]], [[ec4]], [[th2]], [[e1]], [[l2]], [[te3]], [[ec5]], [[ec16]]).
No entry placed here; Australia’s olive growers appear within the California entry ([[ec5]]), and Australia’s whaling is not covered.

The bodies that govern fat across borders: the IWC moratorium, biofuel mandates, the WHO’s trans-fat plan, the end of whaling for profit and plantation workers’ conflicts ([[o6]], [[o7]], [[o3]], [[ec6]], [[l1]]).

sources.intro: The latest folio rests mainly on three books with a point of view — Teicholz on nutrition, Zuckerman on palm, Mueller on olive oil — and on Nestle, Ellis and Kiple.
main: Zuckerman, *Planet Palm* ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x1]], [[w1]], [[l1]], [[o7]], [[e1]]); Kiple for FELDA and sunflower ([[ec7]], [[te2]]).
Mueller for olive oil ([[ec5]], [[o5]], [[o8]], [[l3]]); Nestle for olestra ([[te1]], [[o4]]); Ellis for whaling ([[ec6]], [[o6]]).
Jones and Kiple for vanaspati ([[ec9]]); Mueller for Turkish hazelnut oil and the West Bank ([[x3]], [[c2]]).
Kiple (Berger) for the Middle East’s palm-oil imports ([[ec10]]).
Kiple (Stephens and the Yak chapter) for herders’ milk fat and Himalayan butter ([[ec11]], [[ec12]]).
Teklewold, Uzun, Zhao and Wongyai, in Bedigian’s *Sesame* volume, for Ethiopia, Turkey, China and Thailand ([[ec13]], [[ec14]], [[ec15]]).
contested: The tropical-oil, trans-fat and Women's Health Initiative stories are partisan accounts ([[c1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[l2]]).
Plantation and supply-chain allegations are reported, not adjudicated ([[x1]], [[l1]]).
Mueller's fraud stories are an advocate's; the 1981 outbreak is described only as an ‘industrial additive’ ([[l3]]); canola is only a web lead ([[te3]]).
The Tunisian-oil allegations are investigators’ claims and the charges were later dismissed on limitation ([[x2]]).

The hazelnut-oil case is the investigators’ account, the refiner telling another story ([[x3]]); the West Bank tree counts and attributions are Mueller’s from unnamed sources and politically disputed ([[c2]]).
The import table in Kiple has dashes for years without data, which may mean no figure rather than no imports ([[ec10]]).
The herder entries use late-twentieth-century field figures, so how far back the practices go is not shown ([[ec11]], [[ec12]]).
The sesame chapters give 2005-era figures, the Ethiopian ones from a statistics agency that undercounts commercial farms ([[ec13]], [[ec14]], [[ec15]]).
gaps: The scientific literature on saturated fat and heart disease is not read directly; the other side of the argument (the AHA and mainstream nutrition) has no source in the library.

Brazil, China and Africa’s own oilseed and palm histories, and the 2020s, are barely covered; the Near East has four entries (palm imports, Turkish sesame and hazelnut oil, the West Bank), but Syria, Lebanon, Israel and the Gulf’s own fats, Oceania and Africa beyond Cameroon, Liberia, Tunisia, the herders of Kenya ([[ec11]]) and Ethiopia’s sesame ([[ec13]]) have none.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
*Order* is the largest lane: the guidelines, the trans-fat rules, olestra, the olive standard, the whaling moratorium and the biofuel mandates. *Economy* has the oils; *Lives* has the people.
Teicholz and Zuckerman write as critics; their claims are tagged as such. Treat the nutrition entries as episodes in a live dispute.
The *picture by region* counts the 39 entries: Europe 4, Near East 4, Far East 9, Africa 3, Americas 14, Worldwide 5; none in Oceania. Washington dominates, and Africa has three entries.
